content: The field of view, also referred to as the field of vision, represents the angular extent of the observable environment that can be seen at any given moment. The field of view varies significantly among different species, primarily due to the positioning of their eyes. Humans possess a nearly 180-degree forward-facing field of view, whereas certain bird species have a nearly complete 360-degree field of view. Additionally, the vertical range of the field of view can differ among species. The visual capabilities within the field of view are not uniform and vary depending on the species. For instance, in humans, binocular vision, which is crucial for depth perception, encompasses approximately 140 degrees of the field of view. The remaining 40 degrees of peripheral vision lack binocular overlap, as the images from each eye do not converge in these areas. In contrast, birds with a 360-degree field of view may only have 10 to 20 degrees of binocular vision. Similarly, the ability to perceive color, shape, and motion is not evenly distributed across the field of view. In humans, color vision is concentrated in the central portion of the visual field, while motion detection is more pronounced in the peripheral regions. This is due to the distribution of photoreceptor cells in the retina. The central region of the retina, known as the fovea, contains a high density of cone cells, which are sensitive to color and require bright light for activation. Conversely, the peripheral retina has a higher concentration of rod cells, which are more sensitive to motion and function better in low-light conditions. As a result, peripheral vision is relatively stronger than central vision in dim lighting. Optical instruments, such as binoculars and spotting scopes, often specify their field of view in two formats: angular field of view and linear field of view. The angular field of view is expressed in degrees, while the linear field of view is described as a ratio of lengths. For example, binoculars with an angular field of view of 5.8 degrees may also be described as having a linear field of view of 305 feet per 1000 yards or 102 millimeters per meter. For example, the Wide Field Channel on the Advanced Camera for Surveys aboard the Hubble Space Telescope has a field of view of 10 square arc-minutes, while its High Resolution Channel has a much smaller field of view of 0.15 square arc-minutes. Ground-based survey telescopes generally have much larger fields of view. For instance, the photographic plates used by the UK Schmidt Telescope cover a field of view of 30 square degrees. The Pan-STARRS telescope, equipped with one of the most advanced digital cameras, has a field of view of 7 square degrees. In the near-infrared spectrum, the WFCAM on the UK Infrared Telescope (UKIRT) has a field of view of 0.2 square degrees, while the upcoming VISTA telescope will offer a field of view of 0.6 square degrees. Historically, digital cameras had a smaller field of view compared to photographic plates. However, digital cameras surpass photographic plates in several aspects, including quantum efficiency, linearity, dynamic range, and ease of data processing.
